meta.audience: The reader; the Gentiles directly from verse 22
meta.location: The city of Jordan and the lands north
principles: A warning delivered to the people who will hold the book

world_behind.title: He goes back on his oath
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says he repented of the refusal he made in Mormon 3:11.

world_behind.title: The people misread him
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says they looked on him as though he could deliver them from their afflictions. Mormon 3:11 has him refuse command fifteen years earlier and Mormon 4:23 has him retrieve the records in the meantime, so the people are asking a man who has publicly quit to come back.

world_behind.title: He states his own expectation
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says he took the command without hope, knowing the judgments that were coming. Mormon 3:12 had said his earlier labor was without faith for the same reason. Both times he names the missing thing and does the work anyway.

world_behind.title: He explains the size of the book
world_behind.text: Verse 9 says he writes a small abridgment and dares not give a full account.

world_behind.title: Two reasons are given for holding back
world_behind.text: Verse 9 gives two reasons for writing only a small abridgment: a commandment he had received, and sparing the reader too great sorrow. 3 Nephi 26:11 and Ether 13:13 record the other two occasions a writer in this record is stopped, and neither of those gives the reader as a reason.

world_behind.title: The record has three destinations
world_behind.text: Verses 12, 14, and 15 name the remnant of Jacob, the unbelieving Jews, and the seed of this people.

world_behind.title: The last three verses turn on the Gentiles
world_behind.text: Verses 22 through 24 turn from the Lamanites to the Gentiles and ask how they will stand before the power of God. Mormon 3:17 to 22 had made the same turn, and Mormon 7 is addressed to the remnant instead. The book keeps changing which future reader it is talking to.

words.text: To break up ground, and by extension to distress deeply. Treated at 2 Nephi 9:47. The record uses the word five times and the King James Bible once, at Job 39:10.
A shortened version of a longer record. Treated at 1 Nephi 1:17. It appears three times in the record, and the King James Bible not at all.
Held closely, embraced. The record uses the word twice, here and at Alma 19:30, with none in the King James Bible. Verse 11 has this people clasped in the arms of Jesus.
Repulsive, causing disgust. Treated at 1 Nephi 12:23. The word turns up three times here, and the King James Bible four.
The worship of images or false gods. The record uses the word six times and the King James Bible five. Verse 15 pairs it with unbelief as the cause.
The husks separated from grain and blown away. Treated at 2 Nephi 26:18. Its count is six times, twice in this chapter, in this book, while the King James Bible fourteen.
A rolled length of writing material. Three uses here, and two in the King James Bible. Verse 23 has the earth rolled together as one.

phrases.term: Did repent of the oath which I had made that I would no more assist them
phrases.text: The reversal of Mormon 3:11. He calls the change repentance.

phrases.term: They looked upon me as though I could deliver them
phrases.text: What the people expected of him. Verse 2 says what he expected.

phrases.term: I was without hope, for I knew the judgments of the Lord
phrases.text: Command taken up with the outcome already known. He leads anyway.

phrases.term: Those whose flight was swifter than the Lamanites' did escape
phrases.text: The whole battle reduced to running speed. Nothing else decides it.

phrases.term: I, Mormon, do not desire to harrow up the souls of men
phrases.text: His reason for restraint, given before the reason for writing at all.

phrases.term: All things which are hid must be revealed upon the house-tops
phrases.text: The counter-reason. Matthew 10:27 uses the same image for preaching.

phrases.term: Therefore I write a small abridgment, daring not to give a full account
phrases.text: The book described by its author. Verse 9 gives both reasons in one sentence.

phrases.term: They will sorrow that this people had not repented that they might have been clasped in the arms of Jesus
phrases.text: The grief he expects from his readers. It is grief over a possibility that was open.

phrases.term: They are without Christ and God in the world
phrases.text: The condition stated flatly. Verse 17 says what they had been before.

phrases.term: They were once a delightsome people, and they had Christ for their shepherd
phrases.text: The contrast the chapter is built on. Verse 18 gives the same people steered by no one.

phrases.term: Except ye shall repent and turn from your evil ways
phrases.text: The condition put to the Gentiles. Verse 24 names what follows if they do not.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: An oath reversed, and the reason given is hopelessness
verses.text: The record reports the change of mind and then removes the obvious motive for it: "I did go forth among the Nephites, and did repent of the oath which I had made that I would no more assist them." Verse 2 states what he was not expecting: "I was without hope, for I knew the judgments of the Lord which should come upon them; for they repented not of their iniquities." A commander returns to an army he has already written off, and the record says so before it reports a single engagement.

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: A retreat measured by running speed
verses.text: The record describes the rout with a comparison that has no adjective in it: "those whose flight was swifter than the Lamanites' did escape, and those whose flight did not exceed the Lamanites' were swept down and destroyed." Survival is stated as a function of one variable, and the sentence is built so that both outcomes use the same measure. The record gives no number of dead and no account of the fighting.

verses.label: v. 8–9
verses.title: The writer states what he is choosing not to describe
verses.text: The record marks its own restraint and gives the reason for overriding it: "I, Mormon, do not desire to harrow up the souls of men in casting before them such an awful scene of blood and carnage as was laid before mine eyes; but I, knowing that these things must surely be made known." Two considerations are named and weighed against each other in one sentence, and the writer says which one wins and why: "a knowledge of these things must come unto the remnant of these people, and also unto the Gentiles."

verses.label: v. 12–13
verses.title: The record explains why it is written the way it is
verses.text: Verse 12 gives the audience and the reason for the manner: "these things are written unto the remnant of the house of Jacob; and they are written after this manner, because it is known of God that wickedness will not bring them forth unto them." The style is therefore attributed to a prediction about who will and will not transmit the book. Verse 13 adds that the timing is not the writer's, "this is the commandment which I have received; and behold, they shall come forth according to the commandment of the Lord, when he shall see fit."

verses.label: v. 14–15
verses.title: Two audiences, two stated purposes
verses.text: The record specifies what the book is meant to do in each case. For the first: "they shall go unto the unbelieving of the Jews; and for this intent shall they go, that they may be persuaded that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God." For the second: "that the seed of this people may more fully believe his gospel, which shall go forth unto them from the Gentiles." Persuasion in one case and reinforcement in the other, and the record distinguishes them rather than stating a single aim.

verses.label: v. 17–18
verses.title: The same people described twice, in opposite images
verses.text: The record gives the earlier state in the language of care: "They were once a delightsome people, and they had Christ for their shepherd; yea, they were led even by God the Father." Verse 18 gives the later one in two figures of helplessness: "now, behold, they are led about by Satan, even as chaff is driven before the wind, or as a vessel is tossed about upon the waves without sail or anchor." Shepherd against wind and sea, and the verb is led in both verses.

chapter.title: He calls the reversal repentance
chapter.text: Verse 1 uses that word for going back on his refusal. The oath itself is treated as the error.

chapter.title: He leads knowing the end
chapter.text: Verse 2 says he was without hope. The command is taken up as duty rather than as strategy.

chapter.title: The rout comes down to speed
chapter.text: Verse 7 divides the survivors from the dead by how fast they ran. No other factor is named.

chapter.title: The book explains its own brevity
chapter.text: Verse 9 gives two reasons for holding back. Both are stated to the reader directly.

chapter.title: Restraint and disclosure are held together
chapter.text: Verse 8 says he does not want to harrow souls and that hidden things must be revealed. The abridgment is the settlement between them.

chapter.title: He expects his readers to grieve
chapter.text: Verse 11 describes the sorrow he is counting on. The book is written for people who will care.

chapter.title: The same figure covers before and after
chapter.text: Verses 17 and 18 give the shepherd and the steerless vessel. One people, two conditions.

chapter.title: The last word is to the Gentiles
chapter.text: Verses 22 through 24 turn from the account to its readers. The chapter ends by asking them a question.

applications.title: Go back on a bad oath
applications.text: He repented of a vow he should not have made. Keeping a wrong promise is not integrity.

applications.title: Serve without expecting the outcome
applications.text: He took command knowing what was coming. Faithfulness is not a prediction.

applications.title: Gather people in before the danger arrives
applications.text: Whatever lands they passed by whose inhabitants were not gathered in were burned. The gathering had to happen ahead of the threat, and once it came the window was shut.

applications.title: Decide how much to say
applications.text: He weighed harrowing souls against what had to be known. Both concerns were real and he named them.

applications.title: Limit the account on purpose
applications.text: Mormon writes a small abridgment, daring not to give a full account, partly under commandment and partly so that readers would not have too great sorrow. Judging what a reader can carry is part of writing well, and he states the judgment instead of making it silently.

applications.title: Write for the people who will care
applications.text: He aimed the book at readers who would sorrow over it. Knowing your audience shapes what you leave in.

applications.title: Notice what steering actually takes
applications.text: The image is a vessel tossed on the waves without sail, without anchor, without anything to steer her. Three separate things are named, and losing any one of them produces the same drift.

applications.title: Somebody's prayers are still on file
applications.text: The verse says the Lord will remember the prayers of the righteous which have been put up unto him for them. Prayers offered for people who were not listening are described here as still in force generations later.

questions.text: What promise am I keeping that I should repent of?
Where am I serving without hope of seeing it work?
What am I withholding, and is the reason honest?
Whose loss do I actually grieve?
Where has the Spirit ceased to strive, and did I notice?
How would I stand if asked today?
